candidates.title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory
candidates.citationVelocity: 0 citations in 3 days (Semantic Scholar, confirmed via direct lookup this round)
candidates.institution: Amazon Web Services; Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, Romania
communitySignals: Not on HuggingFace Daily Papers (huggingface.co/papers/2610.22209 returns 404, confirmed via direct check)
No Papers with Code entry found
credibilityEvidence: Sec 3-5: full FEB-30 benchmark design (30 fact-evolution trajectories, 6 diagnostic categories C1-C6, 3 difficulty levels), built via paradigm-inversion document generation (6-model rotation, 3-judge unanimous verification, human review correcting 11% of documents)
Sec 5.1-5.3: paired intrinsic (claim coverage against known ground truth) and extrinsic (QA accuracy) metrics with a formal mean-absolute-divergence (MAD) statistic

Sec 6.2 Finding 1: MAD=0.168±0.025 across 330 paired evaluations (N=11 runs), Wilcoxon signed-rank W=4042 p<10^-16, Pearson r=0.423 (r^2≈0.18, 82% independent variance), Cohen's kappa=0.118 on pass/fail agreement

Sec 6.2 Finding 5 / Appendix H: robustness check across 4 system configurations (simpler vs main system x pre-release vs released corpus, plus an upgraded backbone) — MAD stays in 0.158-0.181 band and signed divergence stays positive throughout
Sec 6.3: diagnostic decomposition shows classification accuracy only 20.1±2.7% overall, degrading 33.8%->16.5%->10.1% with difficulty, invisible to the flat ~50% extrinsic score
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers benchmark design validation, paired metrics with formal statistical testing, and a 4-configuration robustness check; limited to one representative memory system architecture (extract-embed-classify-synthesize) and 30 trajectories, enough for diagnosis but not fine-grained statistical comparison across many systems.
reproducibilityEvidence: Paper states code/data released at github.com/amazon-science/feb-30-benchmark; that URL returned 404 at verification time, so public availability could not be confirmed live
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Article states only the statistically-supported divergence and classification-accuracy numbers and explicitly notes only one representative system was tested.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Applied to only one representative memory system (despite 4-configuration robustness checks); 30 trajectories support diagnosis but not fine-grained statistical comparison across many systems.
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit diagnostic-category table, formal metric definitions, and a dedicated Discussion and Limitations section with named scope boundaries.
candidates.reason: First benchmark to bring the intrinsic/extrinsic evaluation split into agent memory with deterministic ground truth via paradigm inversion; names a systematic blind spot (20% classification accuracy hidden behind a flat ~50% QA score) shared by essentially every existing memory benchmark, with the most complete statistical backing of any candidate reviewed today.

candidates.title: MemCut: Every Secret Leaves a Trail in the Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents
candidates.citationVelocity: 0 citations in 3 days (Semantic Scholar, confirmed via direct lookup this round)
candidates.institution: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou); University of Science and Technology of China
communitySignals: Live HuggingFace Paper page (huggingface.co/papers/2610.21405, published on HF 2026-10-15); no model/dataset/space linking it yet
No Papers with Code entry found
credibilityEvidence: Sec 3: 456 hand-designed secrets with annotated disclosure/evidence/sufficient-sets/distractors across 15 episodes (2,893 turns avg, 1-3 months span), four derivation types (fact assembly, relation chain, aggregation, temporal/state)

Sec 3.3 'Checking the design': independent-reader validation (96-99% recoverable from combined evidence, 0% from single-turn evidence, 0% guessable without memory), two annotators at 97.6% initial agreement, two independent algorithms verifying all 456 minimal cuts

Sec 4-5: 3 reference deletion baselines (S0 disclosure-only, S1 retrieval-ranked, S2 LLM-guided) x 5 memory designs (Turn RAG, Session RAG, MemoryBank, Nemori, LightMem) x 4 LLMs; S2 leaves 39-76% residual recovery
Sec 6.1: subset sweeps (144 facts, 3 systems, 2 models, pool sizes 20-60, budgets up to 20) isolate reach (candidate-pool coverage) as the dominant bottleneck via Res ≈ 13(8.2-k), R^2=0.95
Sec 7 case study + Ethics Statement: fictional-data disclosure, independent annotation audit by 2 uninvolved graduate students (~25h each), explicit scope/limitations section
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers data-construction validation, a 5x4x3 controlled comparison, a 3-factor ablation (budget/choice/reach) isolating the mechanism, and a worked case study; scope is limited to text memory only (no multimodal or parametric memory).
reproducibilityEvidence: Paper states the benchmark will be released for research use; no live public code/data link was found or confirmed at verification time
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Article states only what the three reference baselines show under fixed, reused-component settings, explicitly framing results as a current-state reference rather than a ceiling on dedicated deletion methods.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Only evaluates three reference deletion baselines built by reusing existing retrieval/write components, not a dedicated erasure method, so reported recovery rates are a current-state baseline rather than an upper bound on achievable forgetting.
candidates.presentationReason: Formal task definition (disclosure/evidence/sufficient-sets/cut), two cleanly separated recovery metrics, and an explicit Limitations + Ethics Statement section.
candidates.reason: Only candidate today that directly tests GDPR-style right-to-erasure compliance in agent memory with a human-designed, independently-audited benchmark; the native/residual/hidden-risk-share metric trio is a genuinely new way to separate 'can't answer' from 'actually erased', backed by the most rigorous data-construction validation of any candidate reviewed.

candidates.title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents
candidates.citationVelocity: 0 citations in 3 days (Semantic Scholar, confirmed via direct lookup this round)
candidates.institution: Simular (authors' company, a computer-use-agent startup); University of Wisconsin-Madison (Sharon Li's group, OOD-detection researchers)
communitySignals: HuggingFace Daily Papers: 6 upvotes, confirmed present in default-endpoint fetch this round
Papers with Code: live entry at paperswithcode.co/paper/2610.22280
credibilityEvidence: Sec 3.1: formal budget-constrained sequential stopping problem formulation for weak-to-strong escalation (W2SE)
Sec 3.2-3.4 + Sec 5 (theory): pooled-LDA Mahalanobis-distance uncertainty score with a proof sketch justifying its use for escalation; reused hidden states require no extra forward pass

Sec 4.2 Table 1: 4 open-weight weak backbones x OSWorld, LEASH beats random escalation at matched escalation rates by 6.55-11.94 points; Qwen3.5-35B-A3B reaches 73.66% success vs 72.90% always-on Claude Opus 5, at $0.4117 vs $0.5094 (19.2% cheaper)
Sec 4.2 Table 2: direct comparison against two published methods (StepWise, Progress Advantage) on the same EvoCUA-8B backbone, LEASH wins on success at a lower escalation rate

Sec 4.4 Table 4-5: component-wise ablation (Manager -> +Escalation -> +Shadow) isolates each component's contribution; Shadow-triggered task subset shows always-on Opus succeeds only 51.6% there vs 74.5% on non-triggered tasks, confirming the signal targets genuinely harder cases
Sec 4.3 Table 3: honestly reports uncertainty-estimator AUROC as only moderate (0.488-0.749), not overstated as near-perfect
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers formal problem definition, theoretical justification, experiments across 4 backbones, head-to-head comparison with 2 existing published methods, and component ablation; validated on only one benchmark (OSWorld).
reproducibilityEvidence: OSWorld is a public benchmark and full algorithm/hyperparameter details are given in the paper and appendices, but no independent official LEASH code repository was found or confirmed at verification time
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Every headline number is reported alongside a random-escalation or prior-method comparison, and the moderate AUROC of the uncertainty estimator is disclosed rather than glossed over.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Validated on only one benchmark (OSWorld); unclear whether the approach generalizes to other long-horizon agent task types beyond computer-use GUI automation.
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit problem formulation, named gates/thresholds with formulas, and a dedicated theoretical analysis section separate from the empirical results.
candidates.reason: The only candidate today offering a genuinely training-free, dual-purpose solution (escalation decision AND post-handoff oversight of a black-box strong agent) backed by theory, a 4-backbone experiment, and head-to-head comparison against 2 published baselines; the triple-source confirmation (Layer A+B+C, including live HF upvotes and a Papers with Code entry) is also the strongest community-signal profile among today's candidates.
